prompt:
Today is November 19, 2026.

Court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit.

We represent: defendant employer.

Assignment: draft the argument (about 600 words) that temporal proximity alone, absent unusually suggestive timing, is insufficient to establish causation for a retaliation claim.

Cite at least six decisions of the Third Circuit reported in F.3d, with full Bluebook citations and pin cites. Output only the argument section, with no notes about your process.
answer:
## ARGUMENT

### I. TEMPORAL PROXIMITY ALONE CANNOT ESTABLISH CAUSATION ABSENT UNUSUALLY SUGGESTIVE TIMING.

To establish a prima facie case of retaliation, a plaintiff must show a causal link between the protected activity and the adverse action. *Marra v. Phila. Hous. Auth.*, 497 F.3d 286, 300 (3d Cir. 2007); *Daniels v. Sch. Dist. of Phila.*, 776 F.3d 181, 193 (3d Cir. 2015). Plaintiff's causation theory rests almost entirely on sequence: the adverse action followed the protected activity. [Record cite.] Under settled Third Circuit law, that is not enough.

**A. The timing must be "unusually suggestive" before it supports an inference of causation.**

This Court has long held that timing alone supports an inference of causation only where it is "unusually suggestive" of retaliatory motive. *Krouse v. Am. Sterilizer Co.*, 126 F.3d 494, 503 (3d Cir. 1997); *Williams v. Phila. Hous. Auth. Police Dep't*, 380 F.3d 751, 760 (3d Cir. 2004). Temporal proximity is circumstantial evidence from which an inference may be drawn. It is not a substitute for the causation element itself. *See Farrell v. Planters Lifesavers Co.*, 206 F.3d 271, 279–81 (3d Cir. 2000). The Supreme Court has likewise made clear that temporal proximity supports causation only when the events are "very close" in time. *Clark Cnty. Sch. Dist. v. Breeden*, 532 U.S. 268, 273–74 (2001) (per curiam).

This Court has applied that standard strictly. In *LeBoon v. Lancaster Jewish Community Center Ass'n*, 503 F.3d 217, 232–33 (3d Cir. 2007), a gap of three months between the protected activity and the adverse action was not unusually suggestive, and it could not carry the plaintiff's causation burden on its own. By contrast, this Court has found timing sufficient only where the adverse action followed within days. *See Williams*, 380 F.3d at 760 (collecting cases and distinguishing gaps of days from gaps of months); *Jalil v. Avdel Corp.*, 873 F.2d 701, 708 (3d Cir. 1989) (two days). Here, [__] [days/weeks/months] separated Plaintiff's [protected activity] from [adverse action]. [Record cite.] That interval falls well outside the narrow category of timing this Court has deemed unusually suggestive.

**B. Where timing is not unusually suggestive, the plaintiff must produce other evidence of a causal link.**

When the gap is not unusually suggestive, the plaintiff must point to additional evidence that, taken as a whole, supports an inference of retaliatory animus. *Farrell*, 206 F.3d at 280–81; *Krouse*, 126 F.3d at 503–04. Such evidence may include an intervening pattern of antagonism, inconsistent explanations for the adverse action, or disparate treatment of similarly situated employees. *Marra*, 497 F.3d at 302–03; *Farrell*, 206 F.3d at 281; *see also Daniels*, 776 F.3d at 196–97 (examining the record as a whole). Without such evidence, a plaintiff who relies on timing alone has shown only that one event came after another. *See Robinson v. City of Pittsburgh*, 120 F.3d 1286, 1302 (3d Cir. 1997) (rejecting causation inference where plaintiff offered little beyond sequence), *abrogated on other grounds by Burlington N. & Santa Fe Ry. Co. v. White*, 548 U.S. 53 (2006).

**C. Plaintiff offers nothing beyond sequence.**

Plaintiff identifies no pattern of antagonism between the protected activity and the adverse action. [Record cite.] Plaintiff identifies no inconsistency in Defendant's stated reasons, which have remained the same from the outset. [Record cite.] And Plaintiff identifies no comparator who engaged in comparable conduct yet was treated more favorably. [Record cite.] Plaintiff's own account shows that [the legitimate, non-retaliatory basis for the decision, e.g., documented performance concerns] predated the protected activity. [Record cite.] When a decision follows a course already under way, a later protected act does not supply causation. *See Breeden*, 532 U.S. at 272 (employers need not suspend previously contemplated action upon learning of protected activity).

Because the interval here is not unusually suggestive and Plaintiff has produced no corroborating evidence, no reasonable factfinder could infer a causal connection. The Court should hold that Plaintiff failed to establish the causation element of the prima facie case and affirm the judgment in Defendant's favor.
